The MVP is therefore more than 'documentation plus a version tag' — a small manifest schema change + refusal-to-pool-across-versions is required — and 'do nothing' is only defensible if anchor-relative absolute levels are never compared across independent fits/orders. The cost analysis of a batch MLE (new ADR + optimizer + permanent second estimator) is fair.

R2.claim: The round-1 remedy in `repo:fix-transitivity-gap` ('majority-edge cycle detection plus a scalar inconsistency measure') is not an intransitivity test: a majority edge is just 'observed rate > 0.5', so it counts sampling noise. On the repo's own arena output a transitive BT model reproduces MORE cycles than the data, and an 8-player equal pool yields ~25% cyclic triangles at any sample size. Adopting this as the non-transitivity guarantee would flag noise as cycles.
R2.evidence: /tmp analysis on runs/arena/playable_seed0.json: full 18-entrant pool = 24/800 cyclic triangles (3.0%) vs a BT-model null of 41.5+/-9.2 (z=-1.9); top-8 by elo (14 Elo spread) = 8/56 (14.3%) vs null 13.4+/-3.4 (z=-1.6). Simulation of 8 truly equal players: 13.57/56 cyclic at 30 deals/pair and 13.83/56 at 400 deals/pair (theoretical C(8,3)/4=14). Repo's own doc: tournament-arena.md §9 'pair_diagnostics 的 z 只是烟测 ... <40 Elo 的循环克制会被噪声淹没'.
R2.fix: Gate an edge into the majority graph only when its deal-clustered CI/sign test excludes 0.5 (duel.paired_duel_stats already computes this per pair), then compare the resulting cycle count to a BT-model or random-tournament null (C(n,3)/4) and report the EXCESS. Keep pair_diagnostics as the smoke test. Decision: do NOT adopt a raw majority-edge detector now; add the CI-gated/null-calibrated version later, and only over a pre-registered top-group grid.
R2.correction: Core statistical point is right: a raw 'majority edge' is exactly sign(a_rate-0.5), so near 0.5 it encodes sampling noise, and for m truly equal players the random-tournament baseline is C(m,3)/4. I reproduced the two headline numbers for the repo's own arena file runs/arena/playable_seed0.json: observed majority cycles 24/768 complete triangles (2 exact-rate-0.5 edges: base680k|lvl4, base20k|lvl2; one missing edge greedy|random) and top-8-by-elo (spread 14.36 Elo, exactly the cited 14) = 8/56 = 14.3%. The BT-model null also exceeds the data in my reproduction, so the 24 cycles carry no intransitivity signal. Corrections/overstatements: (1) 'is not an intransitivity test' is too strong - it is an uncalibrated detector that will catch strong cycles; the true defect is that its false-positive floor is ~25% baseline. (2) I could NOT reproduce the full-pool null 41.5+/-9.2 (z=-1.9): resampling the fitted logistic BT model with each pair's actual game count gives 32.1+/-8.5 (z~-0.96). Both give a non-significant z, so the conclusion survives, but the cited null magnitude does not reproduce. (3) The 800 denominator vs my 768 is tie handling (critic counts the 2 tied edges as usable; I drop them). (4) The equal-player 13.57/56 and 13.83/56 assume ties are broken to a side; if exact 0.5 ties are dropped, my 30-game count is ~8.7/56 and 400-game ~12.5/56 (still ~25% *of complete triangles*). (5) The wording 'majority-edge cycle detection plus a scalar inconsistency measure' for repo:fix-transitivity-gap is not in this repo, so the identity of the round-1 remedy is unverifiable; the proposed fix (deal-clustered CI/sign-test gate plus a BT/random-tournament null, keep pair_diagnostics as the smoke test) is sound and its duel.paired_duel_stats reference is real (computes winrate_ci and a deal_sign p-value). The repo doc itself already says this ('pair_diagnostics 的 z 只是烟测 ... <40 Elo 的循环克制会被噪声淹没').

R2.claim: Nash averaging (equilibrium ranking) is the principled answer to cyclic dominance and is cheap in pure Python, but at this repo's data budget its support is not identifiable enough to publish: the Nash mixture swings across many supports under resampling even though the point solver is stable. It also needs an antisymmetric payoff, which the repo's a_rate already provides (a_rate - b_rate = 2*a_rate-1), not the raw score margin.
R2.evidence: Pure-Python fictitious play on runs/arena/playable_seed0.json (18 entrants, 152/153 pairs) gives support {b1,base180k,cp}, stable to solver details (1 distinct support over 8 tie-break seeds at 1k/5k/20k/100k iterations). Bootstrapping the observed pairwise matrix 200 times (per-pair binomial; coarse, no shared-deal correlation) gives 122 distinct supports, mode only 10/200 ['base180k'] (i.e. 95% of resamples pick a different support).
R2.fix: Do not make Nash averaging the published scale. Use it at most as a top-group diagnostic on a pre-registered full-coverage grid with pooled seeds, and report support/weight instability as the uncertainty. Decision: adopt later (diagnostic only), never as the published ranking.
R2.correction: Reproduced independently. (a) The algebra: pair_stats a_rate = (a_wins+0.5*draws)/games, b_rate = 1-a_rate, so a_rate-b_rate = 2*a_rate-1; the meta-game payoff M[i][j]=a_rate(i,j)-0.5 is antisymmetric, so the symmetric zero-sum game has value 0 and NE is a maximin mixture (the raw score margin is not antisymmetric and is the wrong payoff). (b) Pure-Python fictitious play on runs/arena/playable_seed0.json returns support {b1, cp, base180k} = exactly the point support the critic cites, and it is stable at 1k/5k/20k/100k iterations across 8 random tie-break seeds (1 distinct support each time); ~0.05 s per solve. (c) Per-pair binomial bootstrap of the 152-pair matrix is genuinely unstable: over 200 replicates I get 146 distinct supports and the most common support appears only 7/200 (3.5%) (critic: 122 distinct, mode 10/200 ['base180k']; my point support is the mode instead). The exact counts differ by bootstrap seed and tie convention, but the conclusion is confirmed and slightly stronger. Caveat to add: the instability is intrinsic here - the equilibrium value is 0 by antisymmetry and the top group is within ~14 Elo, so the support is exactly the part of the problem the data cannot pin. The fix (use Nash only as a pre-registered top-group diagnostic, report support/weight instability, never as the published scale) is sound.

R2.claim: The round-1 F4/A6 fix ('replace the heuristic with p(1-p) Fisher-information opponent selection ... while satisfying anchor coverage by a pre-planned fixed round-robin') conflates the adaptive matchmaking layer with the published fit. If the info/PFSP-selected games feed the published rating, the fit becomes selection-biased (Arena inverse-weights by 1/P(A_t)) and the paired-deal twin guarantee is broken. The repo already keeps these in separate layers; the fix should name the split instead of proposing p(1-p) as a drop-in for pairing.
R2.evidence: placement/opponents.py:197-226 select_opponent maximises p*(1-p) — used only for the adaptive human-placement session. ladder.py:137-166 plan_games is a fixed counterbalanced round-robin chosen before any outcome. policies.py:202 pfsp_weights ((1-wr)**2+eps) is a TRAINING sampler. duel.py resamples deals for the comparison channel. Round-1 B7 notes Arena's estimator inverse-weights adaptive games.
R2.fix: State the layer split explicitly: p(1-p) and PFSP only for online matchmaking and human placement; the published fit/ranking uses the pre-registered plan_games schedule and deal-clustered h2h (duel.py); never reweight the published likelihood. Decision: adopt now as an explicit non-change — keep plan_games fixed and rating-independent.
R2.correction: Layer separation verified. placement/opponents.py:188 select_opponent does maximize p*(1-p) in its 'info' branch (and Thompson in the first explore_games), and its only consumer is the adaptive human-placement session (placement/session.py:183-189 calls it); ladder.py:115 plan_games builds a fixed, outcome-independent, seat-counterbalanced round-robin (deal seeds drawn before any game); policies.py:202 pfsp_weights = (1-wr)**2+eps is consumed by league.PfspController, i.e. a training sampler; duel.py resamples deals, not games, for the comparison channel. The concern is valid for Design A, whose evaluator.select_opponents_for_candidate feeds adaptively chosen matches into update_match, so the published fit would be selection-biased unless the propensity 1/P(A_t) (Arena/BT-under-adaptive-sampling result) is modelled. Caveat: the specific round-1 F4/A6 wording and the 'Arena inverse-weights by 1/P(A_t)' claim are not in this repo, so I cannot independently verify the critic's characterization of the round-1 fix. The recommendation itself is correct and is essentially an explicit non-change here: p(1-p)/PFSP only for online matchmaking and human placement, published fit/ranking from the pre-registered plan_games schedule and deal-clustered h2h, never reweight the published likelihood.

R2.claim: Neither design nor the round-1 fixes provide any test for a change in the ruler's content (population improving, task/rule change). The repo has already lived through a rules-family change that invalidated every old rating, yet PlayedGame carries no rules/version identity, and tau is a global forgetting factor, not a change-point test; a frozen published ledger simply hides the change. Round-1's A8 fix (hash rules/version) is necessary but it names the trace/manifest, not the estimator input.
R2.evidence: elo.py:100-110 PlayedGame = (seed, seats, scores) only; study.py:26 MANIFEST_VERSION=1 and no rules field. human-elo-plan.md:263 lists '非平稳：真人会进步/手生；窗口/遗忘因子配合轨迹先验' as an open problem. docs/adr/0007-family-comparison.md changed the comparison rules; observation-slimming.md and evaluation-protocol-validation.md headers mark all numbers '规则变更前口径'. tournament-arena.md §9: same lvl4 reads 1392 in one arena vs 1430 in a 400-deal refit (~38 Elo fit-caliber/regime gap) vs the +/-20 Elo CI.
R2.fix: (a) Put a rules/task hash on PlayedGame AND the manifest and refuse cross-version fits (round-1 A8, but it must reach the estimator input, not only the trace JSON). (b) Add a pure-Python per-deal residual CUSUM monitor over anchor/cross games as a first-class metric: a frozen-reference 0.5->0.70 shift is detected in ~50 deals at ~8% pre-change false alarms (K=0.15, h=10 in 0.5-SD units), whereas the online tau update has no alarm channel at all. Decision: adopt now (version key + CUSUM monitor).
R2.correction: The concrete repo gap is real and verified: elo.py PlayedGame = (seed, seats, scores) only (no rules/version identity), study.py:26 MANIFEST_VERSION=1 with no rules field, and the games-out JSONL that fit_ratings can be re-run on has keys seed/seats/scores/subject/opponent/subject_seat/kind and no rules either (the trace JSON does carry version+rules, trace.py:175-177). merge_manifest freezes levels by default, so a population/rule shift is hidden. ADR-0007 documents a real rules-family change that invalidated every prior rating, and tournament-arena §9 gives the 1392 vs 1430 (~38 Elo) fit-caliber/regime gap against a +/-20 Elo CI. So putting a rules/task hash on the estimator input (not just the trace) is a correct, necessary fix. Overstatement: 'neither design ... provide any test for a change in the ruler's content' is wrong for Design B - design-grok §9 item 3 requires task-package versioning ('题库一换,所有 μ 不可跨版本比') and §8 makes it an acceptance condition; round-1 A8 (hash version) is acknowledged by the critic. What is genuinely missing is (i) the version key reaching PlayedGame and (ii) a monotone change-point monitor. The CUSUM calibration is only approximately right: simulating K=0.15, h=10 in normalized (sd=1) units on a 0.5->0.70 per-deal shift gives mean detection ~36 deals (median 31), not ~50, and ~5% false alarms within 50 deals, not ~8%; the direction (tens of deals, single-digit-% false alarms) holds.

If the pool later exceeds ~30 entrants with full pair coverage at >=400 deals/pair, revisit low-rank BT (rank-1 is exactly the current 1-D model) as an exploratory diagnostic with a significance test on the added interaction terms. Decision: never (TrueSkill2, style embeddings), later/conditional (low-rank BT).

R2.claim: Round-1's `code:AB-no-batch-MLE` 'fatal' framing overstates the project impact. For this repo the published comparison channel is already order-free and needs no global MLE: deal-clustered paired h2h plus frozen published levels. A global batch MLE only buys an order-invariant ABSOLUTE table, and its expected effect (~the fit-caliber spread) sits at the CI floor, so it is a reproducibility convenience rather than a correctness precondition.
R2.evidence: duel.py:34-57 plan_duel_schedule builds seat-swapped twins; duel.py:105-255 paired_duel_stats resamples DEALS; duel.py:288 combine_duel_seeds merges seeds; study.py:49-74 merge_manifest freezes levels by default (refit=False). tournament-arena.md §9: the same lvl4 reads 1392 in one arena and 1430 in a 400-deal refit (~38 Elo) vs the +/-20 Elo 400-deal CI; evaluation-protocol-validation.md §5: 20 Elo needs ~807 deals for 80% power.
R2.fix: Downgrade the batch MLE from a fatal blocker to an optional offline publication module (implemented pure-Python per the scipy finding), and instead require that every ranking claim report deal-clustered CIs plus >=2-3 seeds and use duel.paired_duel_stats/combine_duel_seeds as the significance channel. Decision: adopt now (CI/seed discipline), later (global MLE).
R2.correction: All citations check out: duel.py:33-57 plan_duel_schedule builds seat-swapped twins; paired_duel_stats resamples deals; duel.py:288 combine_duel_seeds merges seeds; study.merge_manifest freezes levels unless refit=True; tournament-arena §9 gives 1392 vs 1430 (~38 Elo) against +/-20; evaluation-protocol-validation §5 gives 20 Elo -> 807 deals for 80% power (and notes the pilot's 400-500 figure is 50% power). The conclusion that candidate-vs-candidate h2h comparisons and frozen published levels do not require a global MLE is sound, and downgrading the round-1 'fatal' label is reasonable. But the argument overstates in two places: (1) path/order-dependence is one of the four named drift symptoms in critique/context.md, and the published manifest levels ARE produced by the order-dependent fit_ratings, so the global MLE is not merely an 'order-invariant absolute table' convenience - it directly addresses a stated user requirement; (2) the claim that the MLE's expected effect 'sits at the CI floor' is not supported - the 38 Elo figure is a fit-caliber/regime gap, not a measured order-dependence, and it is ~2x the 20 Elo 400-deal CI half-width, not at the CI floor. Correct framing: the batch MLE is optional for ranking claims (which already use deal-clustered CIs + >=2-3 seeds), but it is the natural remedy for the order-dependence drift symptom and may matter more than the critic allows.

R2.claim: The two-layer design is sold as accuracy-vs-speed, but the repo's latency-critical decision (human placement: a 10-game adaptive session with Fisher-information opponent choice) cannot use the batch layer at all, while the accuracy-critical decision (ranking) is dominated by deal variance, not estimator choice. So the expensive batch layer is justified only as an offline reproducibility report, not on any decision path.
R2.evidence: placement/estimator.py SessionConfig games=10, stop_ci=50; placement/session.py re-fits only the current session's games against a human Prior; the online update is O(seats) and fit_ratings over 32,000 games is 0.45 s. tournament-arena.md §9 38-Elo fit-caliber spread vs +/-20 CI; evaluation-protocol-validation.md §5 resolution table. Round-1 F7 itself notes the designs' constants are calibration thresholds, not detection sample sizes.
R2.fix: Keep the online OpenSkill as the only estimator on the latency path (matchmaking, placement); run any batch MLE/Nash offline, versioned, as a report. Do not gate or place on the batch layer. Decision: adopt now (single online estimator on the decision path), later (offline batch report).
R2.correction: Citations verified: placement/estimator.py SessionConfig games=10, stop_ci=50; placement/session.py:281-291 re-runs fit_session on only self._games (the current 10-game session) against the human prior and rung priors, so the batch layer is indeed not used there; fit_ratings over 32,000 games is 0.424 s and a 10-game refit is microseconds; tournament-arena §9 has the 38 vs +/-20 figure. The recommendation (one online estimator on the latency path, batch MLE/Nash offline and versioned, never gate/place on the batch layer) is sound. Two corrections: (1) the premise 'the two-layer design is sold as accuracy-vs-speed' is a mischaracterization - design-grok §3 and design-gemini 机制三 both already assign the online layer to matching/calibration and the batch layer to the published leaderboard, so there is no decision-path use of the batch layer to correct; this is a strawman. (2) 'latency-critical' is not apt for a 10-game human session that is dominated by human play time, and the session-local fit is O(games), so it is trivially fast regardless. Severity 'minor' is appropriate; the finding is essentially a confirmation of both designs rather than a defect in them.

R2.claim: Round-1's central remedy for the missing batch estimator (math:gemini-replay-is-not-mle, stats:F2, requirements:B-published-mle-layer-does-not-exist: 'Implement a genuine batch estimator ... anchors hard-constrained ... scipy L-BFGS / MM') is ill-posed for this repo: a strong checkpoint virtually always beats the weak RandomBot gauge, so the unregularised anchored MLE is unbounded under separation, and the fix specifies no regularisation, prior, or separation guard. The repo's online estimator only survives because tau (tau>0, elo.py FitConfig) keeps sigma from collapsing; the proposed pure MLE discards exactly that.
R2.evidence: Simulation: /home/amas/.local/src/7g523/.venv/bin/python with /tmp/r2/lib.py bt_mle (MM/Zermelo, one pinned gauge). A player c that beats gauge g in all N games: N=50 gives c_mu = 652.677 (100 iters), 977.045 (1e3), 1302.553 (1e4), 1628.175 (1e5) — monotone divergence, N-independent; 199W-1L converges to 748.586. In the realistic saturated population (g=0, c=600, d=650, e=700, 100 deals/pair, 25 independent samples) the one-gauge MLE c/d/e sd = 74.05/73.18/69.77 (exp_a.py 'saturated' mle). Assumptions/limits: 2-seat only, DGP is the same logistic BT model the MLE fits (p=sigmoid((theta_i-theta_j)/(sqrt2*beta))), so 'truth' = generating strengths and the MLE is the correct estimator by construction; no ties in these runs; saturation of a 600-700 population against a 0 gauge is deliberately harsher than the repo's current spread. This is falsification evidence, not proof.
R2.fix: Do not adopt an unregularised MLE. Use a Bayesian MAP / regularised fit with an explicit prior sd on mu (reuse seven523.elo.Prior), or require at least two pinned/strongly-prioranced anchors so the top of the scale stays identified; specify optimizer, convergence tolerance, and a perfect-separation guard (e.g. refuse to publish when a free id has zero losses and the likelihood ratio to the gauge exceeds a threshold, or report '>= scale max'). Keep the online tau/sigma floor as the fallback and add a regression test that a clean-sheet entrant's published mu stays finite.
R2.correction: Core math is right: an unregularised hard-anchored BT/PL MLE is unbounded under separation (I re-ran lib.bt_mle on clean N-game sweeps: divergence grows with iteration count, N-independent, and a 199W-1L record gives exactly 748.586); the repo's online estimator is finite only because elo.py FitConfig enforces tau>0 plus DEFAULT_PRIOR, which a pure MLE discards. But the 'fatal' / 'virtually always beats the weak RandomBot gauge' premise is overstated for THIS repo: measured candidate-vs-random win rates are 88.5-93.3% (docs/experiments/elo-breakthrough-report.md 4.4), so a clean sheet over the default 100 gauge games is ~0.02-0.2%, and a candidate normally loses some cross games to comparable candidates; it is a separation-guard/robustness gap, not a demonstrated failure. Also 'the MLE is correct by construction' holds only for the critic's logistic DGP: the repo's core is a Gaussian Plackett-Luce (openskill predict_win = Phi(d/sqrt(2*beta^2+sig^2)), beta=100), and on a Gaussian DGP a Gaussian-link (probit) MLE recovers 400/451/504 (sd~20) while a logistic BT MLE returns ~893, so the link choice is itself part of the defect. Round-1's text is not in the repo (critique/ has only context.md and the two designs), so 'the fix specifies no regularisation/prior/guard' cannot be independently verified; design grok 7/9 already calls for hierarchical priors on new models and soft multi-anchor constraints. The recommended fix (MAP using seven523.elo.Prior, separation guard, finite-mu regression test) is sound.

R2.claim: Round-1's 'keep exactly one hard gauge; treat all other snapshots as free parameters or soft prior nodes ... never a second hard gauge' (math anchor-pins fix, stats:F6, repo:both-multi-anchor) leaves the top of the scale effectively unidentified once the population outgrows the gauge: with a single pinned RandomBot the MLE absolute sd at the top is ~70 mu, larger than the 10-20-unit effects the repo gates on, while one additional tightly-known anchor removes most of that. The fix substitutes a very noisy ruler for the stale one it removes, without quantifying the cost.
R2.evidence: exp_a.py 'saturated' (g=0, c=600, d=650, e=700, 100 deals/pair, 25 samples): anchors={g:0} -> MLE c=621.07 sd=74.05, d=671.42 sd=73.18, e=723.93 sd=69.77; anchors={g:0,c:600} -> d=650.63 sd=20.45, e=703.12 sd=17.83 (c pinned). Online reported sigma was only 36.8-38.0. Spread config (g=0,a=0,b=50,c=400,d=450,e=500) MLE sd ~19-21 even with one gauge, so the problem is specifically saturation of the gauge link, i.e. it bites exactly as the ladder improves.
R2.fix: Retain a small set of measured reference snapshots, each as a free/hierarchical node with an explicit tight prior (not a hard stale constant, not deleted): report their posterior and the residual misfit. In the repo seam this is a Prior with a small sigma on chosen ids, or the placement/estimator RUNG_PRIOR_SD pattern. Publish the top-of-scale absolute uncertainty (deal-clustered) alongside every delta-mu, and do not claim a single RandomBot gauge identifies a 600+ population.
R2.correction: Numbers reproduce: under the critic's saturation scenario the one-gauge absolute sd is ~70 (74.05/73.18/69.77) and adding a pinned c drops d/e to ~20/18. But the finding conflates the absolute scale with the differences the repo actually uses: in the same saturated fits the c-d/c-e/d-e differences have sd 18-23 (out_a mle_diffs), and at the repo's historically measured spread (~447 above RandomBot after ADR-0012's -1000 shift, docs/experiments/elo-breakthrough-report.md) the one-gauge absolute sd is only 19-21, comparable to the 10-20-unit effects rather than 3-4x larger. The 70-mu number comes from a 600-700 spread the critic himself admits is beyond the current repo. Round-1's quoted remedy already permits 'soft prior nodes', which is exactly the proposed tight-prior fix, so the claim that it 'substitutes a very noisy ruler' mischaracterises it. Correct framing: keep the tight-prior/reference-node fix and report absolute uncertainty, but present it as a forward-looking gauge-saturation (Fisher information -> 0) risk, not a present 70-mu error.

R2.claim: Round-1's improvement-gate remedy (repo:fix-improvement-gate: 'state thresholds in winrate terms and map them to repo mu via expected_score') does not define a fixed improvement threshold: the winrate -> mu mapping is strongly sigma-dependent, so the same H1 p>=0.55 gate admits anywhere from a ~18 to a ~40 mu improvement depending on how converged the two entrants are. A gate specified in winrate terms therefore cannot be pre-registered as a fixed-size effect without also fixing sigma.
R2.evidence: exp_d.py delta_mu_for_winrate_by_sigma: p=0.55 -> Delta-mu = 17.8 (sigma=0), 18.3 (25), 19.9 (50), 25.1 (100), 39.7 (200); p=0.52 -> 7.1 ... 15.9; p=0.60 -> 35.8 ... 80.1. The repo's fresh entrants sit at sigma~200 and converge to ~35, so the effective threshold moves by >2x over one entrant's lifetime. (Power itself is fine: a fixed-sample deal-clustered test at Delta-mu=20 has power 0.83 at 807 deals, type-I 0.05, matching the repo's own table.)
R2.fix: Define the gate in Delta-mu (or in expected_score against a declared reference sigma) and pre-register it, e.g. 'accept only if the deal-clustered 95% lower bound on Delta-mu exceeds X', reporting the realized Delta-mu and both sigmas. If a winrate threshold is kept, also pre-register the sigma band in which it applies and map through expected_score at that sigma; never reuse the retired 400-logistic 35-Elo constant.
R2.correction: Confirmed and reproduced: p=0.55 maps to 17.8 mu at sigma=0, 18.3 at 25, 19.9 at 50, 25.1 at 100, 39.7 at 200; p=0.52 -> 7.1..15.9; p=0.60 -> 35.8..80.1; fresh entrants start at sigma=200 and converge near 37 (out_a rep_sigma), so the admitted improvement moves >2x over one entrant's lifetime. Critical missing caveat: the design's '35' is on the retired 400-point logistic scale (400*log10(0.55/0.45)=34.9), not the repo's OpenSkill mu scale where the same p is ~17.8 at sigma=0, so there are two confusions in play (sigma and scale); DEFAULT_ELO_SCALE is reporting-only after ADR-0011. The practical spread is somewhat narrower than 18-40 because the SPRT compares consecutive checkpoints with similar sigma, but sigma is neither declared nor pinned, so the pre-registration defect stands. The proposed delta-mu / expected_score-at-declared-sigma gate is correct.

R2.claim: Round-1's transitivity remedy (repo:fix-transitivity-gap: add arena.transitivity_violations with 'majority-edge cycle detection plus a scalar inconsistency measure') has no null model or significance control, so on a genuinely transitive population with finite pair samples it fires spuriously at exactly the sparse-coverage regime the repo's cross schedule is in. It would report cycles that are sampling noise, and the reference 'scalar inconsistency' is likewise uncalibrated.
R2.evidence: exp_e.py transitive_majority_cycle_rate_by_games_per_pair: with a strictly transitive 4-player BT population, P(at least one majority-edge 3-cycle) = 0.145 at 5 games/pair, 0.0037 at 20, 0.0 at 100 (800 trials each). A true rock-paper-scissors cycle sampled at 200 games/pair: the 1-D anchored MLE does not oscillate, it collapses the cycle to a stable gauge-determined order (b-c ~ 42.5 mu, sd 11-14), so the diagnostic's ordering signal is arbitrary rather than 'drift'.
R2.fix: Add a permutation/likelihood-ratio null (or a bootstrap null over outcome resamples) and multiplicity control before declaring a cycle; require a pre-registered minimum games/pair; report the cycle statistic with a p-value and the design effect. For real cycles use a population/Nash-average (or 2-D) model as the diagnostic, and keep the 1-D MLE as the display only.
R2.correction: The missing-null criticism is valid: a majority-edge cycle count with no permutation/likelihood-ratio null, no multiplicity control, and an uncalibrated 'scalar inconsistency' measure can fire on sampling noise, and under a true cycle a 1-D MLE merely picks an arbitrary gauge-determined order (I reproduce b-c ~42.5, sd 11-14 at 200 games/pair). But the specific claim that it fires 'at exactly the sparse-coverage regime the repo's cross schedule is in' is false: ladder.build_ladder/plan_games default cross = games_per_anchor = 100 twin games per candidate pair (src/seven523/ladder.py) and arena.run_arena uses 60, and at those counts the critic's own exp_e gives P(cycle)=0. The defect is real only for close candidates: my paired-twin simulation at 100 games/pair gives 5-12% false positives for adjacent gaps ~30 and 15-26% for gaps ~20, roughly doubling with a per-deal effect. Restate as 'needs a null and multiplicity control, and it is material for close candidates even at the repo's 100 games/pair'; drop 'the repo's sparse regime'.

R2.claim: Round-1's proposed no-drift acceptance test (stats:F8: null injection of identical weights under two ids, require 95% CI coverage of 0 and no outcome-conditional shift) cannot falsify ruler drift because it tests a contrast, not the absolute level. MLE order-invariance is exact and the clone contrast is tight, while the absolute location of the same fit is uncertain by tens of mu, so the suite passes while the ruler has moved/rotted.
R2.evidence: exp_b.py: on a fixed mixed record, MLE shuffle spread = 0.0 for every id, while the online replay spread = a 63.2, c 100.8, d 98.2 (so 'shuffle <1e-6' is an exact, vacuous property). exp_f.py (g=0, c=600, c2=600 identical, d=650, e=700, 30 samples): MLE clone-vs-clone contrast mean -0.78 sd 13.47, but MLE absolute error vs truth sd 53.12 (ratio 3.94); online clone contrast sd 38.4 while absolute error is +113.53 (sd 54.42) with reported sigma 36.92. So a two-clone coverage test can pass while the absolute scale is off/uncertain by ~50-74.
R2.fix: Test the absolute level, not only a contrast: publish a fitted value against a definitional reference (RandomBot=0) plus several measured references, and require the absolute delta to a fixed external reference to lie inside a pre-registered deal-clustered margin; report contrast uncertainty and absolute-level uncertainty separately. Keep identical-id injection as a path/order test only, and never infer 'no ruler drift' from a shuffle test.
R2.correction: Confirmed: a clone-contrast plus order-shuffle acceptance suite is blind to absolute-level bias; MLE order-invariance is exactly 0 (so a '<1e-6' shuffle test on the MLE is vacuous), the clone contrast sd is 13.5 while the same fits' absolute-error sd is 53.1 (ratio 3.94), and the online reported sigma (36.9) understates the online absolute-error sd (54.4), and elo.py's own Rating docstring says sigma is not a standard error. Caveats the finding omits: (a) the 53-mu absolute uncertainty is again the 600-700 saturated scenario; at the current ~450 spread the single-gauge MLE absolute sd is ~20 (out_a 'spread'). (b) Design grok 8 does include an absolute identifiability test against the anchor ('mu-hat within 2 sigma of Delta'), so the suite is not purely contrast-based, but its calibrated sigma* ~= 2.5 openskill units maps to ~60 repo units, so a 2-sigma band is too loose to catch a ~50-mu bias, which reinforces the critic. (c) RandomBot is a fixed program and cannot itself rot; the known large error is estimator bias (the online layer), covered by finding r2-online-inflation. The recommended fix (pre-registered deal-clustered margin on the absolute delta to a fixed external reference; report contrast and absolute uncertainty separately) is correct.

R2.claim: Round-1's 'Remove the mean-subtraction rule and the inflation diagnosis ... it is a mean-zero redistribution' (math:nonzero-sum-is-not-inflation) understates the problem: at equilibrium the online replay exhibits a large systematic level bias relative to the generating model, growing with the skill gap, while the anchored MLE is essentially unbiased. The per-game mean-subtraction rule should indeed be deleted, but deleting the diagnosis is wrong; the online layer's level is population/sigma dependent and the proposed 'reliability/calibration check' against the reported sigma is unsafe because sigma is not a standard error.
R2.evidence: exp_a.py spread (g=0,a=0,b=50,c=400,d=450,e=500, 100 deals/pair, 25 samples): online c=477.72, d=514.51, e=571.88 vs MLE c=401.05, d=448.16, e=502.69 (true 400/450/500). exp_f.py saturated: online absolute error vs truth = +113.53 (sd 54.42) with reported sigma 36.92; MLE absolute error -8.05 (sd 53.12). exp_b.py: online old-entrant a moves -23.03 (sd 38.5) when stronger c,d arrive, MLE moves -0.12 (sd 4.23).
R2.fix: Keep the two-layer split (online only for matchmaking) AND an explicit absolute-level/inflation audit with deal-clustered CIs; delete only the per-game mean-subtraction rule (it fights the gauge), not the inflation diagnosis. Do not validate calibration using openskill sigma; compute realized-vs-predicted win rates against held-out references and report the bias and design effect.
R2.correction: Confirmed, and the bias is not transient: I reproduced online c=477.7/d=514.5/e=571.9 vs true 400/450/500 with the anchored MLE at 401/448/503 (out_a), and re-ran at 400 and 1600 deals/pair where the online top still sits ~+43 to +56 above truth, so it is a genuine level bias rather than prior warm-up. Under a Gaussian DGP matching the repo's own model the online bias is much larger (online c~866-1011 vs a correct-link probit MLE 401.6, sd~20), so the reported sigma is clearly not an SE (36.9 vs online absolute-error sd 54.4). Critical caveat: 'the anchored MLE is essentially unbiased' is conditional on the DGP matching the MLE's link - the critic's logistic Bradley-Terry MLE is itself badly biased (~893 for a true 400) under the repo's Gaussian model, so the fair comparator is a Gaussian/probit MLE, not the logistic one used. Relevance to the real project is high: bootstrap.progress_margin=10 and select_rungs consume the online mu today, so round-1's plan to delete the inflation diagnosis is wrong; the two-layer split plus an explicit absolute-level audit and realized-vs-predicted calibration against held-out references is the right fix.

R2.claim: Round-1 offers two conflicting remedies for batch_recalibrate: 'snapshot before replay ... make the rating step pure (apply_match) and append exactly once' (math:gemini-batch-infinite-loop) and 'Delete batch_recalibrate entirely' (repo:gemini-batch-refit-noop). The first only makes the method terminate; the resulting refit is still a reset-to-default chronological replay with the same 60-100 mu order spread, so it is not a refit and the path-dependence claim remains false. The fix must not present 'make it pure' as repairing the mechanism.
R2.evidence: Design-gemini literal code iterates self.match_history while update_match appends (design-gemini.md:41), confirmed non-terminating in round 1. exp_b.py measures the underlying estimator: on one fixed mixed record the repo single-pass replay spread under 15 shuffles = a 63.2, c 100.8, d 98.2; reset-to-default + replay is exactly fit_ratings from the default prior, so a snapshot+pure-step version reproduces this spread, not an order-free result, and also discards any custom Prior (round-1 repro).
R2.fix: Adopt the deletion remedy: remove batch_recalibrate and the '彻底消除漂移' claim. If a published order-free table is genuinely required, build the regularised anchored MLE (finding r2-mle-separation-unposed) behind an explicit ADR + tool, reading the immutable JSONL log; keep the online replay for matchmaking only and label it order-dependent (as elo.py already does).
R2.correction: Confirmed. design-gemini.md line 41 is one collapsed code block; batch_recalibrate iterates self.match_history while update_match appends to it, so it cannot terminate, and snapshotting would only make it terminate - the body still resets every free node to default_mu/default_sigma and replays the same order-dependent online update (a chronological replay from the default prior, discarding registered node mu), not an order-free refit. exp_b confirms the underlying estimator's shuffle spread (a 63.2, c 100.8, d 98.2). So 'make it pure' must not be presented as repairing the mechanism; round-1's deletion remedy (or a genuinely order-free estimator) is the right call. Caveat: this refutes the implementation, not all of the design's prose - section 1 mechanism 3 does call for a global MLE, so the design is internally inconsistent rather than uniformly replay-based.

R2.claim: The central round-1 remedy -- replace the pseudo-refit with an order-free full-history anchored PL/BT MLE and promote it to the published layer, publishing 'refit-versioned boards' -- trades order-drift for refit-drift. A joint MLE re-estimates every id on every refit, so a fixed model's published mu moves whenever unrelated new games arrive; that is exactly the user's definition of 'the ruler moved'. Worse, in this repo the log is PFSP-selected, so the propensity is outcome-dependent and the fix's fallback 'inverse-probability-weight each game' is not computable from the stored record.
R2.evidence: design-grok.md:220-227 makes both '旧模型不背锅 ... 第一个新模型的公布 μ 几乎不动' (no tolerance) and the full-history MLE acceptance criteria. Reproduced with an anchored Bradley-Terry MLE (gauge B=0), /tmp/attack3.py via `.venv/bin/python /tmp/attack3.py`: with the A/B/C games unchanged, adding D shifts A +1.0225 -> +1.0107 (-0.012) and C -0.4892 -> -0.5100 (-0.021) on a scale where A~1.0; at 20k games/pair the shifts are -0.005/+0.004 but still nonzero, so '几乎不动' is never exactly met. The selection channel is real: src/seven523/policies.py:235 `score = (1.0 - win_rate) ** 2 + epsilon` is computed from cumulative realized wins/draws/losses (policies.py:230-234) and drives PFSP opponent sampling (league.PfspController.record/win_rate), so the next-game propensity depends on the outcomes you would be weighting; the repo stores no pre-game propensity anywhere.
R2.fix: Do not elevate a joint MLE to the published number. Define the published value as a frozen per-snapshot measurement with its CI; use study.merge_manifest(refit=False) (study.py:63-70 already freezes per-id levels) as the published contract, and keep the order-free joint fit as a within-version diagnostic. If joint inference is genuinely wanted, restrict it to a pre-registered balanced schedule (cross twin deals) or log the sampling propensity at each match decision, then weight; never post-hoc IPW from win records.
R2.correction: The arithmetic is real: an anchored joint PL/BT MLE re-estimates every id, and adding D's games moves A and C. I reproduced attack3.py and re-ran at 20k games/pair: A 1.0114->1.0066 (-0.0049), C -0.5202->-0.5167 (+0.0035). Note C's shift sign flips between 1k (-0.021) and 20k (+0.004) and the magnitude ->0, i.e. finite-sample noise, NOT systematic scale drift. With a pinned gauge the scale is identified, so 'the ruler moved' is the wrong description; the movement is O(1/n), sign-unstable and inside the reported CI, and design-grok's own criterion is 'almost no move' (design-grok.md:222), which O(1/n) satisfies. Two further overreaches: (a) the PFSP premise is false for the rating layer -- every fit_ratings consumer (ladder plan_games, arena full cross, bootstrap qualify/mass with uniform random opponents, placement) reads a balanced planned schedule, while PfspController/policies.pfsp_weights (policies.py:230-235, league.py) only drive training opponent sampling and no fit reads league records; propensities are even logged to pfsp_weights.csv at each update (train.py:558-565), so 'no pre-game propensity anywhere' is wrong; (b) the recommended remedy already exists (study.merge_manifest refit=False, study.py:63-70). Severity 'fatal' is unjustified; the correct reading -- freeze the published snapshot explicitly and keep the joint fit as a diagnostic -- is literally the finding's own fix.

R2.claim: The round-1 remedy 'keep exactly one hard gauge and treat every other frozen snapshot as a free parameter or soft-prior node' is not scale-neutral. A reference's sigma enters every opponent update through c = sqrt(sig_c^2 + sig_a^2 + 2 beta^2) and through the division sig_c^2/sig_a^2, so a snapshot's published effect on candidates is set by its own online game count (which determines sigma under tau), not by any definition. This reintroduces a moving ruler inside the published scale.
R2.evidence: /tmp/attack4.py (`.venv/bin/python /tmp/attack4.py`): a candidate that beats a ruler with identical mu=600 in all games is published at mu=1121.932 when the ruler sigma=2, 1135.725 at sigma=48, 1175.551 at sigma=100 and 1277.205 at sigma=200 after 50 games -- a 155-mu spread (14%) from sigma alone; one game moves +98.09 vs +73.17 (/tmp/attack1.py). The repo's own gauge is stable precisely because it is pinned at sigma=0: elo.py:244 `return model.rating(mu=anchors[id_], sigma=0.0, name=id_)`. So the round-1 fix is strictly worse than the convention it would replace.
R2.fix: Allow only two reference classes: a hard gauge with sigma exactly 0 (RandomBot, ADR-0012) and measured snapshots that enter the published fit either as free ids (mu and sigma estimated from their own games) or as an imported fixed (mu,sigma) from an offline measurement that is reported with its CI -- never as a likelihood node whose sigma is an online equilibrium. Set the published scale from the gauge plus candidate-vs-candidate cross twins (ladder cross default, ADR-0012), and report every snapshot's sigma explicitly.
R2.correction: The OpenSkill mechanism is real and attack4.py reproduces it (ruler sigma 2 -> candidate mu 1121.9; sigma 200 -> 1277.2 after 50 all-wins), and elo.py:244 does pin the gauge at sigma=0. But the claim is layer-confused and magnitude-overstated. (1) It applies only where the published number is an online/replay update with a non-zero frozen reference sigma -- notably design-gemini's batch_recalibrate (a replay whose anchor keeps _anchor_sigma; design-gemini.md:15-19,25). It does NOT apply to an anchored BT/PL MLE (design-grok section 7) or to the repo's fitted ratings: the logistic/PL likelihood contains no sigma, so a free id's MLE point estimate is sigma-independent and a soft-prior node's sigma is only the prior SD. (2) The repo is immune: its only reference is the single gauge pinned at sigma=0, all other ids are free or a Prior. (3) The dramatic 155-mu/14% spread uses an all-wins candidate against a near-initial ruler (sigma=200); with realistic balanced schedules (p=0.5-0.6) and a converged free-id sigma (~35 under tau=2, which I measured), the mean candidate shift is only ~5-35 mu (~1-5%), well below the per-run sd (~45). So 'the round-1 fix is strictly worse than the convention it would replace' is not established; the sensible convention is the finding's fix and the repo already does it.

R2.claim: The remedy 'initialize new ids at the scale origin with a wide prior, and propagate parent uncertainty as sigma_new=sqrt(sigma0^2+sigma_parent^2)' is worse than the mechanism the repo already ships and does not remove the selection bias in the inherited mean. Because Delta-mu is proportional to sigma^2, seeding at the scale origin puts a candidate ~500-1000 mu below the pool and makes its first games large, asymmetric, prior/path-dominated moves; adding sigma_parent to the child only widens its own variance and leaves the biased shared family mean intact.
R2.evidence: The repo already does the right pattern: bootstrap.py:326-339 `qualify_priors` enters newcomers from `member.prior()` (the parent's rating at fork time, pool.py:107-109) and then fits a 500-game qualifying slate (bootstrap.py:111 qualify_games=500, :521 priors=priors), so the child 'enter the merge with a measured rating instead of an inherited one' (bootstrap.py:8-13). placement/estimator.py:22-26 already exposes the prior seam (`COLD_START_PRIOR = Prior(500.0, 300.0)`, `RUNG_PRIOR_SD = 30.0`). design-grok.md:37 states the Delta-mu proportional-to-sigma^2 mechanism that makes origin seeding noisy.
R2.fix: Reuse the repo's measured-entry pattern: inherit the parent rating as the prior mean with only the child's idiosyncratic variance, run a burn-in slate before any publish, and never seed at the scale origin. Carry the family-mean uncertainty as a correlated (random-effect) offset when comparing across lineages, rather than inflating the child's own sigma, so sibling comparisons are not contaminated by the parent's selection luck.
R2.correction: Confirmed supporting facts: Delta-mu is proportional to sigma^2 (design-grok.md:37; openskill update), and the repo already uses measured entry -- forks set prior_mu=job.parent.mu (bootstrap.py:743), qualify_priors feeds member.prior() (bootstrap.py:326-339, pool.py:107-109), and each newcomer plays a 500-game qualifying slate (bootstrap.py:111,517-521), exactly the 'measured rating instead of inherited' pattern bootstrap.py:8-13 describes. But the critique is internally inconsistent and partly mis-targeted. If you seed at the scale origin you no longer inherit the family mean, so 'leaves the biased shared family mean intact' applies only to the parent-mean variant; conversely the parent-mean variant is what the repo and design-grok.md:93 already use. Origin seeding is not self-evidently worse: a large Delta-mu for a high-sigma entrant is the desired fast calibration, and the real risk (asymmetric/selected first games) is what design-grok section 6's forced anchor/stratified schedule addresses. Also the repo uses a fixed DEFAULT_SIGMA=200, not sqrt(sigma0^2+sigma_parent^2), so the specific sigma-inflation critique does not describe repo behavior. Net: the recommendation matches the repo; there is no new failure here, and 'major' overstates it.

R2.claim: The remedy for multi-anchor designs -- 'treat additional anchors as hard consistency checks (report the misfit) or as priors with an explicit sigma in the same units' -- does not make the scale identifiable. A soft L2 anchor makes the published free mu a continuous function of the prior weight, which no data can fix; and the hard-consistency-check alternative has no null distribution, so its misfit necessarily grows with n and is not a usable test.
R2.evidence: design-grok.md:194-196 proposes `sum_a (mu_a - c_a)^2 进先验`. /tmp/attack5.py: gauge A1 hard-pinned at 2.0, soft anchor A2 truly 0.5 but targeted at 2.0, free id F truly 1.0. F's estimate sweeps from 0.992 (lambda=0) to 1.038 (1e2), 1.275 (1e3), 1.652 (1e4), while A2 sweeps 0.487 -> 1.734 -- ~0.7 units (70% of the true gap) driven only by the weight. Any finite lambda is an arbitrary prior on the scale, and lambda=0 leaves it unidentified.
R2.fix: Do not soft-pin measured anchors inside the joint likelihood. Either estimate anchor mu freely (its own games identify it) or give it a proper Gaussian prior whose variance comes from an independent measurement, report the anchor posterior and the sensitivity to that variance, and keep only exogenous definitions as hard gauges. Any consistency check must come with its sampling distribution, not a bare pass/fail.
R2.correction: The sensitivity is real: attack5.py reproduces F sweeping 0.992 (lambda=0) to 1.652 (lambda=1e4) and A2 0.487->1.734, and design-grok.md:188-191 does put sum_a (mu_a-c_a)^2 into the prior (note: 188-191, not 194-196). But the framing 'does not make the scale identifiable' is wrong: attack5 has one hard gauge A1, so the scale is identified regardless of lambda; the soft anchor only biases/shrinks the other estimates -- ordinary prior bias-variance, not loss of identifiability. Two more overreaches: attack5 uses a deliberately inconsistent target (A2 truly 0.5, soft-targeted at 2.0) to maximize the weight effect, and 'hard consistency check has no null distribution / not a usable test' is too strong -- a normalized misfit (chi-square/LRT) does have one. Most importantly this is largely irrelevant to the real project: ADR-0012 already established exactly one pinned RandomBot gauge with no multi-anchor path, and no repo code consumes a soft anchor. Keep the finding's fix (free ids or imported fixed (mu,sigma), never online-equilibrium sigma as a likelihood node) as a documentation guard.

R2.claim: The tau remedy ('delete tau=0; use tau>0 and get frozen rulers from write rules; route all fitting through FitConfig') is already the repo's behavior and therefore fixes nothing, while the freeze the designs actually need -- non-anchor mu pinned through the rating pass -- cannot be added to fit_ratings without destroying the pure single-seam contract. The round-1 fix conflates 'don't adopt tau=0' with 'the freeze mechanism'; tau is irrelevant to freezing.
R2.evidence: FitConfig already requires tau>0 with DEFAULT_TAU=2.0 (src/seven523/elo.py:57-63, 144-146). The only write rule in the estimator is `if id_ not in anchors: state[id_] = updated[seat][0]` (elo.py:258-260) and fit_ratings's signature is (games, anchors, priors, config) only -- there is no per-id status. ADR-0011 fixes the seam ('同一个 deep seam 不变') and requires '纯 in-process math -- no torch, no numpy, no paths, no RNG, no clock'. Adding an 'established-frozen' status map would make two fits of the same log depend on mutable pool state, i.e. no longer a function of its declared inputs.
R2.fix: Keep tau>0 and do not touch elo.py's write policy. Implement warm start and freeze at the orchestration layer that already exists: `priors` for warm start (bootstrap.qualify_priors), `anchors` for exact pins (elo.py:244), `study.merge_manifest(refit=False)` for the published freeze (study.py:63-70). If an immutable board is required, freeze the manifest, not the estimator.
R2.correction: Factual core confirmed: FitConfig requires tau>0 with DEFAULT_TAU=2.0 (elo.py:63,139,144-146), the only rating write rule is 'if id_ not in anchors: state[id_] = updated[seat][0]' (elo.py:259-260), fit_ratings takes only (games, *, anchors, priors, config), and tau has nothing to do with freezing -- so 'delete tau=0 / route all fitting through FitConfig' is a no-op relative to the repo (design-grok sections 4/9 recommends tau=0, which the repo forbids; design-gemini uses openskill's default tau>0). Correct that exact pins are expressed by anchors (elo.py:244), warm start by priors, and the published freeze at the manifest layer (study.merge_manifest refit=False, study.py:63-70), so 'freeze the manifest, not the estimator' matches the repo. One overreach: adding an explicit frozen/status parameter to fit_ratings would not inherently make it impure or dependent on mutable pool state -- a set passed as an argument keeps it a pure function of its declared inputs -- so 'cannot be added without destroying the pure single-seam contract' is an opinion, not an established constraint. Severity 'major' overstates a no-op plus a design-preference point.

R2.claim: The remedy 'accept on sample A, rate/publish on an independent held-out sample B; pre-register alpha and the number of generations for alpha spending' fixes the reported number but not the consequence of the gate on training, and alpha-spending is undefined over this repo's stopping rule. The accepted checkpoint is not just published -- it becomes a fork parent and a PFSP pool member, so the gate's winner's curse re-enters the learner's opponent distribution; and because training stops on a plateau, the number of gated candidates is a random stopping time.
R2.evidence: design-gemini.md:47/:57 discard failures and replace Best / enter the pool with the accepted model. PFSP then weights opponents by policies.py:235 `score = (1.0 - win_rate) ** 2 + epsilon` from cumulative session outcomes (league.PfspController in league.py), so a gate-inflated 'best' changes what the learner trains against, independent of how its published Elo was re-measured. Round-1 itself notes the repo has no per-run error budget and no accept gate; the number of candidate comparisons is data-dependent.
R2.fix: Keep PFSP and league weights computed from the league's own session outcomes and never from gate/published values (the repo already does this). Screen with a deal-clustered fixed-sample paired duel or an anytime-valid sequential bound; spend alpha once on a single pre-registered confirmatory endpoint against a fixed reference. Keep rejected checkpoints in the league as opponents, and report the realized false-accept count from the logged candidate list rather than assuming a fixed number of tests.
R2.correction: The general selection-feedback concern is legitimate: design-gemini does discard rejected checkpoints and put accepted ones into the pool (design-gemini.md:47,57), accepted members can become fork parents and training opponents, and the bootstrap loop stops after `patience` unproductive rounds (bootstrap.py:774,828-829), a data-dependent stopping time, so naive alpha-spending would need an anytime-valid bound or a pre-registered cap. The fix's recommendations (clustered fixed-sample/anytime-valid screen, keep rejected ckpts as opponents, report realized false accepts) are sound. But the cited mechanism is wrong: PFSP weights are computed from observed session wins/draws/losses (policies.py:230-235, league.PfspController), not from gate or published Elo, so a gate-inflated rating does not itself reweight opponents; the rating->training channel is pool.trim and fork-parent selection by mu, which the finding does not name. Also the repo has no SPRT accept gate, so this critiques a proposed feature rather than existing code.

R2.claim: The remedy 'report a full pairwise matchup matrix with deal-clustered CIs and multiplicity control; declare a cycle only when significant' is data-infeasible at this repo's resolution and mostly duplicates an existing diagnostic. The repo's default cross schedule gives ~50 deals per pair, whose CI half-width cannot see a 20-Elo cycle; a full K-candidate matrix at the needed resolution is a large, mostly underpowered programme, and arena.pair_diagnostics already provides the deal-clustered observed-vs-model screen.
R2.evidence: src/seven523/ladder.py:118-119 `games_per_anchor=100` (games) and build_ladder resolves cross=games_per_anchor (ladder.py:567-568), so the default pair plays 100 games = 50 deals. docs/experiments/head-to-head-pilot.md:20 gives a 400-deal 95% CI half-width of 18.8-20.9 Elo, so 50 deals is ~19.6*sqrt(400/50) ~= 55 Elo. A full pairwise matrix at 400 deals is K(K-1)/2 x 400 deals (K=20 -> 76,000 deals). src/seven523/arena.py:241-279 `pair_diagnostics` already computes an observed-vs-model z with `deals = games // 2` and is labelled 'a transitivity smoke test'.
R2.fix: Do not schedule the full matrix. Extend pair_diagnostics with a multiplicity-corrected threshold and one scalar inconsistency (max |z|, or count of pairs exceeding it), aggregate it across runs from the stored JSONL, and run a single targeted 3-cycle confirmatory test (A>B>C>A, shared-deal slate) only for the frontier top-r when a z survives. Keep the pairwise matrix as a diagnostic, not a release gate.
R2.correction: Confirmed: build_ladder resolves cross=games_per_anchor=100 games = 50 deals per candidate pair (ladder.py:118-119,567-568), arena cross=60 = 30 deals; arena.pair_diagnostics already computes a deal-clustered observed-vs-model z with deals=games//2 and is labelled a transitivity smoke test (arena.py:241-279), so a full matrix largely duplicates it; and ~19.6*sqrt(400/50) ~= 55 Elo is the right CI scaling for 50 deals. Overstated: 'data-infeasible' is wrong -- a full K=20 matrix at 400 deals/pair is 190 pairs / 76,000 deals, and the repo's own pilot measures ~14 s per 400-deal pair (head-to-head-pilot.md:20), i.e. order 45 min on one GPU, not infeasible. Also 400 deals is not 'cannot see a 20-Elo cycle': the same doc says 400 deals can 'barely distinguish' ~20 Elo (and <10 Elo needs 1500-2000 deals); it is the 30-50-deal default that cannot. The recommended fix (extend pair_diagnostics with a multiplicity-corrected threshold plus one targeted 3-cycle confirmatory test) is reasonable.

R2.claim: The versioning remedy ('hash the rules into every PlayedGame and refuse to fit across versions; if continuity is needed run an overlap-based equating study and publish the measured offset with CI') does not identify an offset. Equating two rule scales requires assuming the overlap models' strengths are unchanged across the rule change, which is exactly what a rule change invalidates; and the gauge itself is version-bound, since RandomBot's expected score against a fixed checkpoint is a win rate that changes with the rules, so a cross-version mu offset is confounded with the gauge.
R2.evidence: PlayedGame carries only seed/seats/scores (src/seven523/elo.py:96-113) -- no version field. docs/adr/0007-family-comparison.md consequences: '规则变更前产生的所有数字 ... 不可与新规则结果混比' and '旧 ckpt 是在旧规则下训练的，新规则下的强度必须重测'. ADR-0012 defines the gauge by RandomBot's outcomes, which are rules-dependent. So 'measured offset with CI' is circular for mu, and the repo's actual resolution was to declare non-comparability, not to equate.
R2.fix: Make the scale identity include the rules version (scale_id = rules_version + gauge_id), start a fresh board per version, and report cross-version comparisons only as head-to-head win rates between an old-ruler reference and the new gauge on a shared bridge slate, explicitly not as a mu offset. If a version must be bridged, state the parameter-invariance assumption and test it with held-out overlap models, not with the same games used to fit.
R2.correction: Confirmed factual base: PlayedGame carries only seed/seats/scores (elo.py:100-113), no rules-version field; ADR-0007 states pre-rule-change numbers are not comparable ('规则变更前产生的所有数字 ... 不可与新规则结果混比') and that old ckpts must be re-measured under the new rules; ADR-0012 makes the scale RandomBot-based, hence rules-dependent; and the repo's actual resolution is to declare non-comparability, not equate. But 'does not identify an offset / circular' is too strong: overlap equating does identify an offset under an explicit, empirically testable anchor-invariance assumption (overlap models' relative strengths unchanged across versions); it fails because that assumption is dubious for ADR-0007's substantive family-comparison change, which is an empirical failure, not logical circularity. The recommendation (scale_id = rules_version + gauge_id, fresh board per version, cross-version comparisons only as head-to-head win rates on a shared bridge slate) is exactly ADR-0007's position and should be adopted; treat 'measured mu offset with CI' as unsupported shorthand.
